newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stock liberalisation seen as temporary lift.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stock liberalisation seen as temporary lift.

text.p: The Taiwan government's decision to raise the ceiling on foreign ownership of Taiwan stock shares will give the market a psychological boost but longer-term benefits may be limited, analysts said on Monday.
The central bank and finance ministry announced on Monday they had agreed to raise the ceiling on foreign-held stock equity to 25 percent of total market value by the end of 1996, up from 20 percent.
The two agencies, in a joint statement, also adjusted the ceiling on holdings by any single foreign investor in any one listed stock to 10 percent from 7.5 percent.
Analysts said the liberalisation measures could pull the local stock index out of its doldrums temporarily, but said it would not be enough to trigger a bull run.
"Any news of market liberalisation is good news to investors and the market probably will react immediately," said Joe Chiou, senior analyst at Taiwan Securities Investment.
"However, the change is really not that big and it is not effective until the end of the year," Chiou added.

Michael Hung, senior analyst for Nikko Securities, predicted Taiwan's index might see a 50-point gain on Tuesday before hitting a strong barrier at 6,500. The index lost 36.11 points on Monday to close at 6,453.98.

"Foreign ownership in the market right now is a little less than five percent, so the rise from 20 percent to 25 percent is not going to make of a difference beyond the psychological level," Hung said.

Analysts said the rise in the investment ceiling for a single foreign investor was the more significant of the two relaxations, as it may prompt major foreign investors to pour more funds into blue-chip shares.

"It is unlikely that overall foreign investment would ever test the 25 percent limit, but big investors like Morgan Stanley may increase weightings of certain blue-chip stocks now that the 7.5 percent limit has been raised," Chiou said.

Major shares in the market, especially those in the heavily weighted financial and electronic sectors, have attracted strong foreign buying since Morgan Stanley began including Taiwan in its global emerging market stock indices on September 2.
Most of the 78 stocks listed by Morgan Stanley are considered blue chips, or large-capital shares with a leading performance in Taiwan's various industries.
Taiwan has said it would seek to raise the foreign investment ceiling to 50 percent in June 1997 and then fully scrap the limit in December 1997.

The government says it wants to turn the island into a regional financial centre like Hong Kong or Singapore by liberalising its economy to attract foreign investment and corporations' regional operation hubs.
